Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

A display device comprises counter electrodes configured to be used as common electrodes for displaying and scan electrodes for touch sensing, a first scan circuit which scans gate lines, and a second scan circuit which scans the counter electrodes. In the display device, one frame period includes a write period for continuously scanning one screen and a touch sensing period existing between the write period and a write period in the next frame. The second scan circuit includes a shift register unit and a switch unit. The switch unit includes a seventh thin-film transistor which outputs a DC drive signal to an output node and an eighth thin-film transistor which outputs an AC drive signal to the output node. A second control signal for fixing the voltage of a third retention node to which the gate electrode of the seventh thin-film transistor is connected is inputted in the write period.

The display device uses counter electrodes that serve dual functions: they operate as common electrodes during display operation and as scan electrodes during touch sensing. A first scan circuit scans the gate lines, while a second scan circuit scans the counter electrodes.

Each frame includes a write period, during which one complete screen is continuously scanned, followed by a touch-sensing period that occurs before the write period of the next frame. The second scan circuit includes a shift-register unit and a switch unit. Within the switch unit, a seventh thin-film transistor outputs a DC drive signal, while an eighth thin-film transistor outputs an AC drive signal. During the write period, a control signal fixes the gate-node voltage of the seventh thin-film transistor, thereby stabilizing its switching state and ensuring appropriate output of the DC drive signal.
outputs.L4:
The display device includes a display panel in which a plurality of pixels are arranged in a matrix. Each pixel is connected to a gate line and a signal line and includes a pixel electrode. Counter electrodes are disposed opposite the pixel electrodes and are shared by multiple pixels. In addition to generating the electric field used for image display, the counter electrodes function as touch-sensing electrodes, thereby reducing the number of components required in the panel.

Operation of the device is divided into write periods and touch-sensing periods. A first scan circuit sequentially drives the gate lines during each write period so that image signals supplied through the signal lines are written to the corresponding pixels. A second scan circuit drives the counter electrodes in coordination with the first scan circuit. Thus, the gate lines and counter electrodes can be controlled independently while remaining synchronized with the overall display and touch-detection timing.

The second scan circuit includes thin-film transistors connected to the counter-electrode lines. Depending on the operating period and the selected electrode, these transistors supply either a substantially constant DC voltage or a time-varying AC drive signal. During a write period, a selected counter electrode may be held at a prescribed reference potential so that image data can be written accurately. During a touch-sensing period, an AC signal is applied to one or more counter electrodes, and the resulting capacitive response is detected to determine whether a finger or another conductive object is present.

The second scan circuit further includes a retention node that controls the relevant switching transistors. While pixel data is being written, the voltage of this retention node is fixed at a predetermined level. Preventing the retention-node voltage from floating or changing unintentionally suppresses erroneous switching, leakage-induced fluctuations, and interference between the display-driving and touch-sensing operations. The counter-electrode voltage therefore remains stable during image writing, while the required AC waveform can be output reliably during touch detection.

By coordinating the first and second scan circuits in this manner, the device can alternate between display writing and touch sensing without significant mutual interference. The shared use of the counter electrodes simplifies the panel structure, while selective DC and AC driving and stable retention-node control improve image quality, touch-detection accuracy, and overall operating reliability.

## The Power of “The”

“The” is one of the smallest yet most important words in the English language. Known as the definite article, it points to a specific person, place, object, or idea. When we say “the book,” we mean a particular book that is already known or understood. This simple word gives language clarity and precision.

Despite its ordinary appearance, “the” can also create a sense of importance. Expressions such as “the future,” “the truth,” or “the one” suggest something unique and meaningful. It connects speakers and listeners by relying on shared knowledge: both understand what is being discussed.

Without “the,” many English sentences would sound unclear or unnatural. Its frequent use demonstrates how even the shortest words can play an essential role in communication.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a concise technical abstract for a display device that uses counter electrodes as both common display electrodes and touch-sensing scan electrodes.
counterfactuals.output: A display device integrates touch sensing with image display by using counter electrodes as both common display electrodes and touch-sensing scan electrodes. The counter electrodes are divided into independently driven segments coupled to a drive circuit. During a display period, the segments receive a common voltage for cooperation with pixel electrodes to form an image. During a touch-sensing period, selected segments receive scan signals, and resulting capacitance changes are detected to determine a touch position. Sharing the counter electrodes reduces electrode count, wiring complexity, and device thickness while enabling coordinated display and touch operation with reduced interference.

counterfactuals.prompt: Explain how the first and second scan circuits, shift register unit, switch unit, and seventh and eighth thin-film transistors operate during the write and touch-sensing periods.
counterfactuals.output:
### Write/display period

- The **shift-register unit** advances a start pulse in response to the display clock and generates scan pulses one row at a time.
- The **switch unit** is set to the display path, coupling the shift-register outputs to the **first and second scan circuits** while isolating the touch-sensing path.
- The **first and second scan circuits** alternately or sequentially drive their associated scan lines—typically two groups of rows. An asserted scan pulse turns on the pixel switching TFTs of the selected row, allowing source/data-line voltages to be written into the pixel capacitors.
- The **seventh and eighth TFTs** operate as routing/isolation switches. In this period, the TFT associated with the display-scan path is turned on and the TFT associated with the touch path is turned off, so normal row scanning is not disturbed by the touch circuitry.

### Touch-sensing period

- Normal row writing is suspended, and the **shift-register unit** is stopped, reset, or driven with a touch-scan timing sequence.
- The **switch unit** changes state, disconnecting the ordinary display-scan signals and connecting the scan electrodes/lines to the touch-driving or touch-readout path.
- The **first and second scan circuits** then select the touch electrodes or electrode groups in sequence. One circuit may supply the touch excitation while the other holds nonselected lines at a reference level or assists in selecting another group.
- The states of the **seventh and eighth TFTs reverse**: the display-routing TFT is turned off to isolate the pixel-writing circuitry, and the touch-routing TFT is turned on to pass the touch excitation or sensed response.
- After sensing, the switch unit returns to the display state, the shift register resumes normal row-by-row operation, and pixel writing continues.

Thus, the same scan-line infrastructure is time-shared: the shift register and scan circuits perform display addressing during the write interval, while the switch unit and seventh/eighth TFTs reconfigure and isolate the circuitry for touch detection during the sensing interval.

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe a display apparatus with integrated touch sensing in which a second scan circuit selectively supplies DC and AC drive signals to counter electrodes, specifying the relevant TFTs and control signal used during the write period.
counterfactuals.output:
A touch-integrated display may include pixel electrodes, counter electrodes that also serve as touch-drive electrodes, a first scan circuit for writing image signals, and a second scan circuit for driving the counter electrodes. For each counter electrode, the second scan circuit includes:

- a **DC-selection TFT** connected between a DC common-voltage line and the counter electrode; and  
- an **AC-selection TFT** connected between an AC touch-drive-signal line and the counter electrode.

During the pixel write period, a **write/display control signal** turns the DC-selection TFT on and the AC-selection TFT off, so that the selected counter electrode receives the DC common voltage. During the touch-sensing period, the TFT states are reversed, allowing the second scan circuit to selectively apply the AC touch-drive signal to the counter electrodes.
